messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Car Similarity: Similar cars
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tariq is a 30-year-old Iraqi-American tax inspector who presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that left him, by his own account, fundamentally altered. Divorced and living alone in a one-bedroom apartment, he arrived at the intake appointment having taken a rideshare rather than driven himself — a detail he offered unprompted, as though anticipating judgment.

The accident occurred on a Friday evening in late autumn. Tariq had been driving home from a work function when a driver who had been drinking ran a red light and struck the driver's side of his sedan at considerable speed. He recalls the sound of the impact — a compression of metal so total it seemed to arrive before he could register it as sound — and then the smell: sharp, unmistakable, the sweet-sour reek of alcohol drifting through the broken window from the other vehicle. He was conscious throughout. Emergency responders took nearly forty minutes to reach him. He spent that time unable to move, watching traffic continue on the adjacent lanes, the other car crumpled against his door. He was hospitalised for several days with a fractured clavicle and lacerations, then discharged into a life that no longer felt continuous with the one before.

In the weeks that followed, Tariq found that the world had reorganised itself around the accident. Driving became impossible — not merely difficult, but genuinely unthinkable. He had not been behind the wheel since the night of the collision, and being a passenger produced a vigilance so consuming that he would grip the door handle and scan every intersection for cars moving at angles that suggested they might not stop. He had come to believe that any car resembling the one that struck him — a dark, mid-size sedan of a particular make — carried within it a kind of ambient danger, and he would track such vehicles on the street even when walking. The smell of alcohol, encountered at a colleague's farewell gathering or drifting from a restaurant bar, could stop him mid-step, his body momentarily convinced it was somewhere else entirely.

His work as a tax inspector requires him to attend field audits at various commercial premises, and it was here that the disruption became most visible. Several audit sites are restaurants and hospitality venues. On two occasions over the past months, Tariq excused himself abruptly when he detected alcohol nearby — once telling a client he needed to take a phone call, standing outside in the cold for several minutes before he could return. His supervisor has noted that he appears distracted and has asked whether he is managing his caseload. Tariq has not disclosed the accident's ongoing effects to anyone at work. He is certain, in a way he finds difficult to articulate but impossible to dismiss, that he is no longer capable of the focused, methodical analysis that once came naturally to him — that whatever made him competent has been damaged in some way that will not repair itself.

At home, he spends long stretches of the evening absorbed in his phone — games, social media, video content — moving from one to the next in a way that feels less like enjoyment and more like maintenance, keeping the mind occupied so that it does not turn toward what it turns toward when left alone. He has been eating very little, sometimes skipping meals entirely, without fully understanding why. He startles at sounds with a frequency that embarrasses him: a door closing in the hallway, a car horn outside, a colleague setting down a mug too firmly on a desk. He is on guard in a way that does not ease, even in rooms he knows to be safe.

What frightened Tariq most, and what finally brought him to seek help, was not the hypervigilance or the avoidance but something quieter: the growing conviction that he had lost access to the emotional life he once had. He described a numbness that he found more disturbing than pain. He had come to believe that he would never feel the ordinary texture of things again — satisfaction, warmth, ease — and it was this, more than anything else, that he hoped someone might be able to tell him was wrong.
